title: The eve of the summit
hookLine: like the last night of a festival, slow and full
tomorrow: the scroll ends, then rolls back. what's the first word again?

cards: The car is packed. The mezuzah is wrapped in a sock in the glovebox. Noa's phone keeps lighting up: the group is going for late-night pancakes, last chance, come on.
And from the kitchen comes the smell of her mom's brisket, which Rachel only makes for holidays. Noa stands in the hallway between the two, feeling guilty in both directions.
There's a festival built for exactly this kind of night. After the seven days of Sukkot comes one more day, the eighth, Shemini Atzeret. Why add a day when the festival is already over?

teach.b: Leviticus gives the day almost no instructions. In the JPS translation, "it is a day of solemn assembly." No booth to sit in, no branches to wave.
Just the day. Rashi reads the name, atzeret, as holding back, and tells a parable. A king invites his children to a feast that lasts several days.

teach.h: STAY WITH ME ONE MORE DAY.
teach.b: When the time comes for them to go, he says: my children, please, stay with me one more day.

teach.h: YOUR LEAVING IS HARD FOR ME.
teach.b: Your leaving is hard for me. That's the whole holiday. Not a new ritual.
Not a bigger celebration. One more day, together, because parting is hard. Here's what the tradition gives a night like Noa's.

The last night isn't for cramming in everything left on the list. It's for staying a little longer at the table you're about to leave. Slow, full, and a little sad, and the sadness is part of the love.
And notice who's asking in the parable. Not the guests.

teach.h: THE HOST ASKS YOU TO STAY.

teach.b: The one being left is allowed to say: stay. Noa can still get pancakes. But some readers would say: brisket first, and don't rush it.

how: Shemini Atzeret, the eighth day after the seven days of Sukkot, is a festival day with few rituals of its own; Rashi explains it with the parable of a king who asks his children to stay one more day because their parting is hard.

games.q: what does “the eve of the summit” mean?
o: the night you rush to finish everything on the list
the last night: slow, full, and staying a little longer
the night you pack the car and get to bed early

games.q: one more day — tap the pairs.
p: your leaving is hard for me

s: Shemini Atzeret is packed with its own special rituals
Leviticus calls it a day of solemn assembly, with almost no instructions.
in Rashi's parable, it's the host who asks the guests to stay
my children, stay with me one more day; your leaving is hard for me.
the last night is for cramming in everything left undone
the parable asks only for one more day together.

games.q: it's your sister's last night home before she moves across the country. she wants to see everyone; your dad just wants dinner. you're the tiebreaker. what does Rashi's king suggest?
o: dinner first, unhurried; the one being left is allowed to say stay.
let her see everyone; a last night should be as full as possible.
skip both and help her pack; that's the practical choice.
games.why: Rashi's king asks his children for one more day, because parting is hard. the last night is for staying a little longer, not cramming.

practice: Wherever you are this evening, choose one sound to listen to: dishes in a sink, a voice in another room, the hum of the house, traffic far off. Listen to it the whole time, without doing anything else.
When your mind runs ahead to tomorrow, come back to the sound, and stay one more minute.

wordCard.voice: The eve of the summit: the last night, slow and full, like the extra day a king asked his children to stay.

orig.note: Hebrew: the eighth day of assembly, right after Sukkot.

carryVoice: Your line: the last night. Slow and full, and a little longer at the table than you planned. Thirteen of fourteen; tomorrow, the top.

sources.q: it is a day of solemn assembly

sources.ref: Rashi on Leviticus 23:36 (atzeret: 'I have held you back'; the parable of the king asking his children to stay one more day)
